extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy (metaphysics/ethics), scholars of Schopenhauer
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Schopenhauer's account of the will as thing-in-itself, its relation to phenomena, freedom and necessity, the ethical consequences (assertion/denial of the will), and the epistemic basis of moral psychology (character, motives, repentance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Immortality as thing-in-itself (not temporal permanence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the individual phenomenon of the will has a temporal beginning and end, the will itself as thing-in-itself is outside time and not affected by temporal cessation; death destroys the illusion of separateness of consciousness and so, as thing-in-itself, the individual is timeless (this is not immortality in the temporal sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer contrasts temporal permanence (a doctrine of immortality) with the timelessness of the will/thing-in-itself: permanence and transitoriness are predicates valid only in time, whereas the will lies outside time. He warns that this is not the consolation sought by egoism (the phenomenological survival of the individual), but a metaphysical statement: the individual's exemption from death belongs to him only as thing-in-itself. Example phrasing: 'death destroys the illusion which separates his consciousness from that of the rest: this is immortality.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical knowledge can overcome the terror of death
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosophical knowledge of the nature of the world (recognising the will as thing-in-itself) can, insofar as reflection dominates feeling, overcome fear of death by placing the individual on a higher standpoint viewing the whole rather than the particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a psychological/therapeutic claim: one who has assimilated the philosophical truths Schopenhauer advances can await death with indifference because he recognises himself as the will mirrored in the world. Examples invoked: Krishna's counsel to Arjuna, Goethe's Prometheus. Caveat: such knowledge may not prevent immediate fear when death is actually present; its power depends on the individual's capacity for reflection to override feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assertion of the will vs denial of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'assertion of the will' means that, even when the will's nature is known, volition continues and life is willed deliberately; the 'denial of the will to live' means that upon attaining full knowledge volition ceases because particular phenomena no longer act as motives and the will suppresses itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer distinguishes two possible reactions of the will upon knowledge: continued willing with knowledge (assertion) and suppression/self-denial (denial). He notes these are expressed in conduct and behaviour (living knowledge), not merely abstract propositions, and that both proceed from knowledge but in different practical manifestations. He promises to exhibit examples later (ethics, action) and warns not to prescribe either universally since the will is free in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of the will as thing-in-itself vs necessity of phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The will, as thing-in-itself, is not subject to the principle of sufficient reason and is therefore free (a negative concept: denial of necessity). All phenomena, however, are governed by the principle of sufficient reason and are therefore necessarily determined. This resolves the apparent contradiction between freedom and necessity: the world-as-phenomenon is necessary, the will-in-itself is free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer presents a metaphysical taxonomy: phenomena = objectivity of will = determined by sufficient reason; will-in-itself = free. Practical implication: although objects (including human behavior as phenomenon) are necessary in causal chains, their origin (the character/Idea) is an expression of a free will. He notes this freedom cannot normally show itself in phenomena except in special cases (leading to apparent contradictions) and that understanding requires distinguishing these levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: The person/phenomenon is not free; individual actions are necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the will in itself is free, the person as phenomenon (empirical character manifest in time and space) is never free: individual actions follow necessarily from character and motives under the principle of sufficient reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer stresses that the empirical multiplicity of actions conforms to law like any natural phenomenon; individuals feel a priori that they are free, but experience and reflection reveal actions follow necessarily from the coincidence of character and motive. He references philosophical arguments (e.g., Priestley, Kant) and warns against confusing the transcendental freedom of the will with empirical libertarian freedom (liberum arbitrium indifferentiæ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between intelligible character and empirical character
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligible character = the will as thing-in-itself in a definite individual (outside time, indivisible, unchangeable); empirical character = the manifestation of that will in time and space (actions, bodily structure) subject to the principle of sufficient reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer uses this Kantian distinction to explain how a timeless will can underlie time-bound, law-governed behavior. He gives the tree analogy (one tendency manifesting repeatedly in different parts). Practical consequence: empirical conduct can be studied inductively to infer character, but this does not alter the intelligible character itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusion of empirical freedom due to intellect's ignorance of intelligible character
rubrics_metrics.description: The intellect perceives a choice as open because it lacks access to the intelligible character that determines the will; thus the apparent ability to choose otherwise is an epistemic illusion (subjective 'can' means 'can for the data known to us').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer illustrates with a hesitating vertical beam ('it can fall either way') and with deliberation: while deliberating the intellect lacks data about how the will will decide, so both options seem possible. Objectively, once motives and intelligible character are considered, the decision is determined. Anti-pattern: mistaking the subjective appearance of multiple possibilities for actual ontological indeterminacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motives move only insofar as they are known (causa finalis moves secundum esse cognitum)
rubrics_metrics.description: For motives (final causes) to influence action they must be known; their causal efficacy depends on their being presented to the agent's knowledge, not merely on their objective reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer quotes the scholastic formula 'causa finalis movet non secundum suum esse reale; sed secundum esse cognitum' and gives examples: a man's wealth and the sight of others' want only motivate action if he knows how he can employ his wealth. Imaginary circumstances (beliefs) can act like real ones (e.g., belief in reward in afterlife motivates benevolence). Practical implication: education and belief-shaping change what motives take effect, without changing the will itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge can change means and conduct but not the underlying will
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction and corrected knowledge may alter the means by which the will pursues its unchanging end (and thus change observable conduct), but they cannot change the fundamental willing itself (the will remains what it is).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mohammed's paradise pursued either in the real world or in imagination; knowledge can cause a shift from one set of means (prudence, fraud) to another (abstinence, justice) while the inmost striving remains constant. Schopenhauer cites Seneca ('velle non discitur') and stresses the practical limit of moral education: you can teach better means, not a different ultimate will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repentance is corrected knowledge, not a change of will
rubrics_metrics.description: Repentance arises from a correction of knowledge about the relation between an act and one's inmost intention; one repents (and may make amends) because one recognises, through increased knowledge, that past actions were not in conformity with one's will, not because the will itself has changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer distinguishes true repentance (rectified knowledge leading to amends) from mere anguish of conscience (pain at the recognition of one's nature). He notes that one cannot truly repent in the sense of altering what one has essentially willed, only repent of actions done under false conceptions. He warns that people sometimes stage 'hasty errors' as deception; genuine repentance manifests in attempts to make amends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character reveals itself over time as knowledge increases ('velle non discitur')
rubrics_metrics.description: A person's empirical conduct changes with increasing knowledge (motives come into awareness), but these changes reveal rather than alter the underlying will; one is initially 'innocent' only because one lacks knowledge of one's true nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer explains that features of character, especially bad tendencies, become stronger or more visible with age as motives become known; alternations in outward behavior (impetuous youth to sober age) reflect changing knowledge of circumstances and motives, not a change of the will. Practical consequence: moral evaluation should account for epistemic development over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rare manifestation of will's freedom in phenomenon can appear as holiness/self-renunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: In exceptional cases the freedom of the will (thing-in-itself) may show itself in the phenomenon by abolishing the nature underlying the phenomenon, creating a contradiction within the phenomenon that manifests as holiness and self-renunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer suggests that while normally the will's freedom is inaccessible in phenomena, in the highest cases (when the will attains self-knowledge and relates itself to its Ideas) the will may suppress itself and this suppression appears within time-bound phenomena as ethical ideals like self-denial. He defers full explanation to later parts of the work but signals this as the metaphysical source of religious/ethical self-renunciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art springs from the presence of high degree of self-knowledge (comprehension of the Ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: When man attains the high degree of knowledge in which the will attains full self-consciousness (comprehension of the Ideas), art arises from this actual presence of knowledge as a manifestation of the will's mirror in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer links aesthetic production to a certain level of cognitive attainment: art emerges when the will's Ideas are comprehended as a pure mirror of the world. This is presented as one of the practical consequences of intellectual development of the will (to be developed elsewhere in the work).
